name: Wahls Protocol

lead: The Wahls Protocol is a food-based plan created by physician Terry Wahls, who has multiple sclerosis. It is a modified Paleolithic diet emphasising dark leafy greens, sulfur-rich vegetables, deeply coloured fruits and vegetables, quality meat and fish, and omega-3 fats, with grains, legumes, dairy and sugar limited.

In a looksmaxxing context, people adopt it as a whole-food, lower-sugar, lower-processed eating pattern that may support leanness, energy for training and clearer-looking skin. Published research on the diet concerns multiple sclerosis symptoms such as fatigue; it has not examined cosmetic outcomes.

paras: Followers build meals around large amounts of vegetables, quality animal protein, fish and healthy fats, and remove grains, legumes, dairy and processed foods. Wahls describes stricter tiers of the plan that cut carbohydrate further, including a ketogenic version. Practitioners typically follow it for months, tracking energy and weight.

The diet is restrictive and low in carbohydrate, and in multiple sclerosis trials participants lost weight, which a 2025 review flagged as a concern for people with ALS. The protocol is not a substitute for medical treatment, and people with medical conditions or low body weight usually consult a clinician first.

angle.text: Followers use the protocol as a clean-eating framework. Cutting sugar, grains and processed foods while eating many vegetables can lower calorie intake and body weight, which is the route by which it could show up in appearance.

lead: The Wahls Protocol is a diet and lifestyle plan created by Terry Wahls, a US physician and clinical professor who was diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis in 2000 [1]. She described it in the 2014 book The Wahls Protocol: How I Beat Progressive MS Using Paleo Principles and Functional Medicine, followed by a 2017 cooking book [1].

The plan is a modified, low-carbohydrate Paleolithic diet that emphasises leafy greens, colourful fruits and vegetables, high-quality animal proteins and omega-3 fats, and limits grains, legumes, dairy, sugar and processed foods [2]. Wahls's version also restricts eggs and nightshade vegetables [1].

People attracted to physique and skin goals sometimes adopt the protocol as a whole-food approach to leaner body composition and general vitality. Its published research is about multiple sclerosis and ALS, where reviewers have discussed it, and not appearance outcomes.

paras: The diet is described as a modified Paleolithic diet that emphasises dark green leafy vegetables, colourful fruits, high-quality animal proteins and omega-3 fatty acids while limiting grains, legumes, dairy, sugar and processed foods rich in omega-6 fats [2]. Wahls's own description also excludes eggs, nightshades and starches [1].

Wahls says she used the diet while her own MS progressed to the point she used a wheelchair, and she reported improvement in her symptoms [1]. She spread the approach through a TEDx talk, the 2014 book, a cookbook and clinical trials she runs [1]. A TEDx talk on the topic was mentioned in a T Nation forum thread on coconut oil and Alzheimer's [3].

A 2025 ALSUntangled review noted plausible mechanisms involving inflammation, oxidative stress and mitochondrial function, but found no demonstration of slowed ALS progression, and reported an average 7.2 percent BMI loss in MS trials, which it called a concern in ALS; it did not endorse the diet for that purpose [2].

A 2020 Cochrane review found no research supporting diet or vitamin supplementation for treating MS, and critics such as neurologist Steven Novella have disputed Wahls's claims, while pointing to reliance on anecdote and her sale of related products [1].

A case study described a 62-year-old woman with MS who combined low-dose naltrexone with the Wahls Protocol and reported fewer, milder chronic migraines [4]. The ALSUntangled review summarised the diet's research in ALS and MS trials, including the weight loss seen [2]. No study has examined the protocol for cosmetic outcomes.
